before: Reliable comparison of seismic phase pickers requires traceable data identities and inspectable relationships between training observations and derived predictions. We present a reproducible evaluation workflow linking waveform fingerprints, earthquake-source groups, out-of-fold feature construction, model provenance and numerical verification. An exhaustive audit of the local STanford EArthquake Dataset archive uniquely matches 2,234 retained waveforms to 1,477 sources. A fixed source-disjoint split contains 330 test records from 221 sources. Fresh replay loads all 106 checkpoints, reproduces 18,528 out-of-fold and 1,980 test feature tensors, and recovers 70 test prediction sets; independent calculations reproduce 1,260 metric rows. Synthetic examples demonstrate rejection of invalid source membership, augmentation lineage, feature order and artifact bytes. Temporal stacking and a PhaseNet-style baseline provide a case study of component access. On this fixed split, stacking achieves accepted-pick F1 scores within 100 ms of 0.8268/0.5536 for compressional/shear arrivals with three components and 0.8134/0.2686 with vertical input alone. The shear-phase difference is 0.2850, with a conditional source-cluster 95% interval of 0.2293–0.3418. The baseline has a supported compressional-phase advantage; primary shear-phase method-comparison intervals include zero. The contribution is an executable connection between identity, data lineage and evaluation, rather than a new stacking algorithm. Historical development exposure prevents an independent-confirmation claim. One fixed split, limited unseen-station observations and the unavailable original extraction recipe constrain predictive interpretation and reconstruction.

before: The study asks three connected questions: can retained waveform exports be linked uniquely to their source records in the local archive; can those identities be traced through grouped fitting, OOF feature assembly and fixed-model replay; and what conclusions about three-component versus vertical-only input survive the documented evaluation and development constraints? The informatics contribution is the executable connection between these stages and its observed verification on a retained seismic dataset. Grouped cross-validation, stacking and hashing are established techniques. Their individual novelty is not asserted, and successful replay is distinguished from independent predictive confirmation.
after: The study addresses three questions: RQ1, can retained exports be linked uniquely to waveform records and earthquake sources in the local archive; RQ2, can those identities be followed through grouped fitting, out-of-fold features and fixed-model replay; and RQ3, what component-access and method comparisons are supported on the fixed split? The contribution is a case-tested integration of identity resolution, executable membership and feature contracts, and numerical verification. These established techniques are connected across the pipeline rather than proposed as new algorithms. Successful replay is distinguished from independent predictive confirmation.

before: Evaluation used 330 test records from 221 sources and tolerances of ±50, ±100, and ±200 ms. The primary policy accepted finite detected or uncertain picks. Accepted picks within tolerance were true positives; accepted picks outside tolerance contributed both a false positive and a false negative. Missing picks contributed false negatives. Thus FP = Naccepted − TP and FN = N − TP. Detected-only sensitivity and seed-42 confusion counts are reported in Online Resource 1, Tables S10 and S7. The primary policy retains lower-confidence candidates to expose the coverage–timing tradeoff; accepted coverage must not be interpreted as accurate detection.

Thus FP = Naccepted − TP and FN = N − TP. Detected-only sensitivity and seed-42 confusion counts are reported in Online Resource 1, Tables S10 and S7. The primary policy retains lower-confidence candidates to expose the coverage–timing tradeoff; accepted coverage must not be interpreted as accurate detection. Every test record contains P and S reference arrivals; there are no noise-only records. Here false positives count mistimed accepted picks, and precision is not a continuous-stream false-alarm measure.

before: For reuse, three evidence levels must remain distinct. Matching waveform and artifact identities establishes consistency of the computational objects. Source-disjoint fitting and OOF membership establish the specified exclusions within v2. Neither establishes independence from earlier research decisions involving these observations. This distinction connects data identification (Duerr et al. 2011) with validation design, while preserving the difference between the forecasting analyses of Jover-Alfaro et al. (2026) and the phase-picking case study here. The contribution is most useful as an auditable evaluation procedure whose limits are visible, rather than as a claim that additional pipeline complexity improves predictive skill.
after: The checks separate artifact consistency, exclusion of specified dependencies within the corrected workflow, and independent predictive confirmation. Only the first two are established here. Waveform fingerprints connect exported records to archive entries, while membership and feature contracts connect those identities to fitted models and predictions. This complements dataset interfaces such as SeisBench (Woollam et al. 2022) and the entity/activity/derivation perspective of PROV-DM (Moreau and Missier 2013); it is not a replacement for those tools or a claim of PROV conformance. For transfer, users must define a scientifically appropriate grouping key and test which dependencies remain outside it (Roberts et al. 2017).
